home.subtitle: I design and build enterprise systems on .NET: order management, workflow orchestration and integration. And I work on how a team can use AI in delivery while people still decide what reaches production.
home.signature: AI produces · people decide · the engine verifies. <goldpath>Goldpath</goldpath> lays the path, <specdrift>SpecDrift</specdrift> keeps it honest.
home.stackDescription: Diagram: software delivery as five stacked layers (intent, spec, code, gates and runtime), each showing who acts on it: AI produces, people decide, the engine verifies.
layers: What must be true. A person owns and signs every rule; nothing unsigned reaches a sprint.
AI drafts the specification from the rules, a person signs it. Open questions keep it out of delivery.
AI writes the code against a test that exists before it, and every commit carries its rule id.
Deterministic checks, no model in the loop: drift, parity with the legacy system, rule and code moving together. Nothing unverified gets past.
Every business event carries its rule id, so the running system explains itself.

about.title: Hi, I'm Ömer.
about.metaDescription: Ömer Çelik is a Lead Developer at DefineX, building enterprise software on .NET since 2018: order management, business process orchestration and integration, and governed AI in software delivery.
body: I'm a Lead Developer at DefineX, building enterprise software on .NET since 2018. Mostly the systems large organizations run on every day: order management, business process orchestration, and the integrations that hold them together.

I like owning a system from the first architecture decision until long after go-live. Screens, services, processes, data, integrations, releases. If it breaks in production, it's mine to fix. As a team lead I set the technical direction, agree on standards with the team, review the work, and plan delivery so big changes reach production in small, safe steps.

My focus now is on how regulated organizations can adopt AI in software delivery without losing control. Someone has to own what AI is allowed to do, and model access should go through a gateway, governed like any other API. Business rules, specifications and code should change together, so the documentation stays current and knowledge doesn't depend on one person. And the test strategy has to be strong enough to decide what reaches production, especially when a legacy system is being replaced.
I build open source tooling for this with Claude Code, MCP servers and agent skills. This site is where I write it down, show it running, and keep an honest record of the work.
